label: Title
notes: Open the lecture by emphasizing that a moduli space is not merely a catalogue of examples. The chapter asks when two Einstein metrics should be considered the same, what the local coordinates on the set of solutions look like, and where infinitesimal calculations fail to integrate into honest families. The visual arc is quotient, slice, obstruction, rigidity, and examples.

label: Chapter Map
notes: Use this slide as the roadmap for the source span. Each topic answers a different moduli question: what the points are, what equivalence relation is imposed, which tangent vectors are real, and which examples have either room to move or no room at all. The map also prepares students for the difference between a formal tangent space and a genuine local parameter space.

label: Einstein Structures
notes: The phrase Einstein structure means the metric is remembered only up to the symmetries that do not change the geometry under discussion. Scaling and diffeomorphism both matter, but they play different roles depending on whether the Einstein constant is normalized. Stress that moduli begins when one stops treating coordinate presentations as new geometry.

label: Quotient Picture
notes: This quotient diagram is intentionally finite-looking even though the true spaces are infinite dimensional. The large ambient space is the space of metrics, the blue locus is the Einstein equation, and the teal orbits are diffeomorphism directions. A moduli point is what remains after collapsing the orbit directions without losing the transverse solution data.

label: Surfaces
notes: Surfaces give the cleanest sanity check because the Einstein equation is equivalent to constant Gaussian curvature. In dimension two, topology separates the spherical, flat, and hyperbolic cases, and moduli is dominated by conformal or Teichmuller data rather than by a complicated Ricci tensor. This is the first place to distinguish normalized geometry from scale.

label: Flat Manifolds
notes: For flat manifolds, the curvature equation disappears but the quotient problem does not. One still has to divide by affine symmetries and by the discrete holonomy data that identifies points in Euclidean space. The lattice picture is a useful reminder that zero curvature can still produce a nontrivial moduli problem.

label: Linearization
notes: Now move from examples to local analysis. An infinitesimal deformation is a symmetric two-tensor that survives the linearized Einstein equation after gauge directions have been removed. The displayed operator should be read as a schematic memory device: the Lichnerowicz Laplacian, curvature action, and Einstein constant combine to decide first-order motion.

label: Gauge Slice
notes: The slice picture is the local replacement for the impossible task of choosing one representative from every orbit globally. The vertical arrows are pure diffeomorphism directions, while the horizontal slice is where the elliptic deformation problem is posed. This prevents students from counting coordinate changes as geometric deformations.

label: Deformation Complex
notes: The complex organizes the local tangent calculation. Vector fields generate infinitesimal diffeomorphisms, symmetric tensors represent metric variations, and the linearized Einstein operator tests whether the variation preserves the equation to first order. The middle cohomology is the first approximation to the local moduli space.

label: Formal Integrability
notes: First-order solutions are promises, not completed families. Formal integrability asks whether a tangent vector can be extended order by order into an actual curve of Einstein metrics. The amber obstruction layer in the diagram represents the moment where quadratic or higher terms can stop an infinitesimal deformation from becoming real.

label: Premoduli
notes: A premoduli space is the local analytic object obtained after choosing a slice and solving the equation there. It is not yet the final moduli space because residual isometries may still identify points inside the slice. This distinction is especially important near metrics with nontrivial symmetry, where the quotient can have orbifold-like behavior.

label: Einstein Constants
notes: The Einstein constant is a coordinate on the type of solution, but it is not independent of scaling. Rescaling the metric changes the constant inversely, so normalized moduli problems usually fix volume, scalar curvature, or the sign of the constant. The slide should make students cautious about comparing families before a normalization has been chosen.

label: Rigidity
notes: Rigidity is the case where the local moduli space collapses to a point after quotienting. Analytically, this often appears when the gauge-fixed linearized operator has no kernel in the relevant complement. Geometrically, it means every sufficiently nearby Einstein metric is obtained from the original one by the permitted symmetries.

label: K3 Endpoint
notes: K3 surfaces sit at the opposite emotional temperature from rigid examples. They show that special holonomy and Ricci-flat geometry can produce rich families rather than isolated points. The period-domain sketch is not a proof; it is a visual way to remember that cohomological data controls a large part of the moduli description.

label: Lab
notes: Use the lab slide to turn the lecture into a diagnostic exercise. The three prompts ask students to separate gauge from geometry, first-order from integrable, and scale from true Einstein type. Encourage short answers that name the exact quotient, kernel, obstruction, or normalization being used.

label: Recap
notes: Close by returning to the basic question: what does it mean to vary an Einstein structure? The answer has several layers: quotient by diffeomorphisms and scaling, solve an elliptic linearized equation, check nonlinear obstructions, and then interpret examples through rigidity or flexibility. This gives students a portable template for reading later moduli problems in geometry.
